title: The Only Classroom Rules You'll Ever Need
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin rejects elaborate or trendy classroom management gimmicks in favor of simplicity, arguing that the goal of classroom management is simply to eliminate distractions and poor behavior so a teacher is free to inspire students. He recounts a phone call with a former student who could not even remember his fourth or fifth grade teachers, using it as a warning that without solid classroom management, a teacher's impact fades into forgettability. He lays out four criteria for effective classroom rules — clarity, a limit of four or five rules, coverage of every possible behavior, and specificity — then shares the four rules he has used for years: listen and follow directions, raise your hand before speaking or leaving your seat, respect your classmates and your teacher, and keep hands, feet, and objects to yourself. He closes by cautioning against mixing academic expectations into behavior rules, arguing the two should be kept separate for clarity.
points: Effective classroom rules should be clear, limited to four or five, cover every possible behavior, and be specific.
Rules themselves don't motivate compliance — the teacher's consistent enforcement does; there is 'no magic' in the rules alone.
Behavior expectations should be kept separate from academic/learning expectations to avoid confusing students.
The four recommended rules are: listen and follow directions, raise your hand before speaking or leaving your seat, respect classmates and teacher, and keep hands, feet, and objects to yourself.
quotes: The goal of classroom management is to eliminate distractions, disruptions, and poor behavior, so you are free to inspire your students. The results are happy and high achieving students.
But as we were talking, it saddened me to hear him say that he couldn’t remember his fourth or fifth grade teachers. He couldn’t even describe them to me.
Clarity trumps all. Your students must clearly understand your rules in order to follow them.
Make sure your rules cover every eventuality. You can’t enforce a behavior unless it falls under the banner of one of your rules. Doing so is confusing and unfair to students.
Remember, the rules themselves don’t motivate students to follow them. You do.

Notice that these rules are related to behavior only. I know some teachers like to include learning expectations as well, like, for example, Complete Work On Time or Work Independently. But combining them with behavior rules can be confusing.
